claims.text: Premelting and melting in HEA nanoparticles are primarily governed by selective surface segregation driven by differences in elemental surface energy.
Elements with higher surface energy preferentially occupy sub-surface positions.
A sub-surface layer enriched in high-surface-energy elements forms a core-shell-like structure that stabilizes the nanoparticle.
High-surface-energy atoms beneath the surface increase the dissolution potentials of adjacent surface atoms.
Increasing surface-atom dissolution potentials delays nanoparticle premelting and melting.
High-surface-energy atoms migrate beneath the surface during segregation.
Nanoparticles enriched in high-surface-energy elements at sub-surface sites will have a higher melting-onset temperature than randomly distributed controls.
Nanoparticles enriched in high-surface-energy elements at sub-surface sites will exhibit slower premelting dynamics than randomly distributed controls.
The proposed initial nanoparticles have a disordered FCC structure and a homogeneous or nearly homogeneous elemental distribution.
Composition changes or processing can be used to promote or suppress surface segregation while particle size and shape are held constant.
The mechanism applies to disordered-FCC HEA nanoparticles with compositions similar to CrMnFeCoNi.
The mechanism applies to certain Pt-based HEA nanoparticles.
Surface processes typically dominate the relevant behavior above 1000 K.
The proposed relationship may fail in nanoparticles with crystal structures other than disordered FCC.
Nanoparticle size effects can overwhelm surface-segregation effects.
Reduction potentials and local atomic coordination affect surface-atom dissolution behavior.
Diffusion rates and local chemical ordering contribute to the proposed premelting and melting behavior.
